transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62m
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood Sr. SE), Jonah Ellis (Redwood SE), Lena Torres (OceanByte Head of ML), Raj Patel (Platform Lead), Samantha Cho (Dir Product), Mike O'Neil (CTO)

Summary (auto): Scope POC for conversation service: characterize bursts, model token-skew, define benchmarks and schedule pilot.

00:00 - Alicia Park: okay everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
00:05 - Lena Torres: yep loud and clear, thanks Alicia.
00:12 - Alicia Park: quick intro — I'm Alicia, AE on this account, Marcus and Jonah from our engineering team. The goal today is to map out your workload so we can size a POC — success criteria, what to measure, and timeline.
00:30 - Marcus Chen: hi all, i'll mostly focus on the benchmark design and replay tooling. quick note: some of the terms we use, QPS versus concurrency, we want to nail those down early.
00:47 - Raj Patel: hi, Raj. From platform side we care about peak concurrent sessions more than steady QPS, because our frontend multiplexes many short chats.
01:05 - Samantha Cho: product is focused on 2 main flows: short assistant style replies (~20-60 tokens) and long-form summarization that can be 400-1200 output tokens. so there's a big skew.
01:28 - Marcus Chen: that's helpful, token-skew means we can't just do average token math, need distribution percentiles. do you have historical token histograms?
01:45 - Lena Torres: we can pull them, yes. we'll need to scrub any PII first. expecting to share by next week.
02:03 - Jonah Ellis: perfect. for replay we prefer a little replay harness that preserves inter-arrival times and concurrency shape — bursts matter a lot for tail latency.
02:20 - Mike O'Neil: question — what kind of tail metrics should we sign up for? p95 is fine but p99 and p99.9 are what break our UX.
02:36 - Marcus Chen: agreed. for this POC we recommend measuring p50/p95/p99 latency for generation, and p99 token-synthesis time when using KV cache warm-up scenarios. also track cold-start vs warmed cache.
02:55 - Alicia Park: i'll add that to success criteria: p95 < 300ms for short replies, p99 < 1s for short; long-form we expect higher but we'll set throughput targets.
03:12 - Raj Patel: clarify — short replies are end-to-end developer call or just model compute time?
03:22 - Marcus Chen: we'll measure both. model compute (inference) and end-to-end including network and queueing. we'll break down token cost too. Redwood console shows token-level cost so you'll be able to map to cost per 1k tokens.
03:45 - Samantha Cho: what's our baseline? we currently run on a self-hosted cluster with mixed A100 and some T4s for lighter workloads. the latency is erratic during marketing spikes.
04:02 - Marcus Chen: that matters; hardware heterogeneity drives variance. our benchmark will include homogeneous Dedicated runs and a Hosted run to compare.
04:20 - Lena Torres: can you support private deploy? we have strict data residency and KMS requirements.
04:29 - Alicia Park: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and VPC peering for on-prem or private cloud. we'll share SOC2 and security docs.
04:45 - Raj Patel: what's the usual approach to simulate user think-time and session multiplexing? we have many small chats that interleave.
05:00 - Jonah Ellis: use a two-tier generator: one generator for session-level arrival and another for per-message token distribution. the replay will maintain session affinity so KV caches warm correctly.
05:18 - Marcus Chen: we recommend capturing the token distribution by percentile (10/25/50/75/95/99) and also a QPS time-series with 1s granularity for peak capture.
05:36 - Mike O'Neil: how do you handle very long outputs? we have multi-turn where assistant produces 800-1200 tokens. that's the heavy tail.
05:48 - Marcus Chen: for long outputs we plan to benchmark using both streaming and non-streaming generation, measure per-chunk latency, and consider quantized model variants to reduce memory pressure. we'll also test sequence-length dependent kernel selection during the run.
06:10 - Lena Torres: timeline wise what do you need from us?
06:16 - Alicia Park: ideally two weeks of anonymized traffic samples + the list of critical SLOs. we'll deliver a benchmark template within 48 hours after this call.
06:28 - Raj Patel: two weeks is fine, we'll start prepping. question about cost: do you have estimates for Dedicated vs Hosted at 1M tokens/day?
06:40 - Alicia Park: we'll put in a ballpark in the spreadsheet; final numbers depend on batching, cache hit rate, and quantization.
06:52 - Samantha Cho: can we try a small-scale replay first — like a 24-hour condensed run with bursts to emulate a week?
07:00 - Marcus Chen: yes, a condensed replay with acceleration factor is typical. we'll also do a full-time-window replay for accuracy on tail metrics.
07:15 - Raj Patel: any restrictions on sample format?
07:20 - Jonah Ellis: CSV or newline JSON with request id, session id, prompt tokens, response tokens, timestamps; if you provide token counts per item that's best.
07:36 - Lena Torres: we'll produce newline JSON with token counts.
07:42 - Mike O'Neil: what about concurrency limits inside the private environment? we run heavy mem footprint models so we need to understand GPU memory per replica.
07:55 - Marcus Chen: good point. our sizing will include memory footprint per model variant and per-sequence allocation (KV cache). we'll give recommended replica counts and autoscale policies.
08:12 - Alicia Park: success criteria recap: (1) p95/p99 latency targets for short and long flows, (2) cost per 1k tokens under target, (3) stable tail under 99.9th quantile during bursts, (4) reproducible replay run showing similar metrics to prod samples.
08:35 - Samantha Cho: that sounds right.
08:41 - Marcus Chen: technical note — when measuring tail latency, please instrument queueing latency separately; sometimes tail is due to queuing, not model slowdowns.
08:57 - Raj Patel: we also want a canary rollback plan if Dedicated performs worse after rollout.
09:05 - Alicia Park: we'll include canary A/B policies and automatic fallback to a lower-capacity model variant.
09:18 - Jonah Ellis: regarding caching: we'll test both prefix caching and full KV cache between turns to see hit-rate impact. please include multi-turn sequences in your samples.
09:35 - Lena Torres: will do.
09:40 - Marcus Chen: a few more questions about burst topology: are bursts correlated across users or localized to a subset of endpoints?
09:52 - Samantha Cho: marketing pushes cause global bursts; but support flows create localized sustained concurrency. both exist.
10:04 - Marcus Chen: okay we'll design two profiles: global spike bursts and sustained localized hot paths.
10:12 - Mike O'Neil: can Redwood's runtime do model variant fallback mid-request if capacity drops?
10:20 - Alicia Park: we have automatic fallback at request-routing time; mid-request fallback isn't ideal, but we can do fragmented responses or preemptively route to a smaller variant. we'll document tradeoffs.
10:35 - Raj Patel: about security again: KMS integration — we use Azure Key Vault; is that supported?
10:42 - Jonah Ellis: yes, we support Azure KV and AWS KMS with customer-managed keys in Private deployments. we'll send the integration guide.
10:52 - Marcus Chen: benchmarking details: we'll run three phases — warmup (cache priming), steady-state replay, and stress spike test. each phase will capture token-level metrics and tail latencies.
11:08 - Samantha Cho: for the stress spike test, can we define a spike of 10x baseline for 2 minutes and then a cooldown? that's representative.
11:16 - Marcus Chen: yes, we can script that. also capture a gradual ramp and an instantaneous jump to see autoscaler response.
11:28 - Lena Torres: do you provide replay tooling as a container? we want to run inside our VPC for private deployments.
11:35 - Marcus Chen: yes, we'll provide a replay container and a config file; you can run it in your VPC or we can run from Redwood with secure peering.
11:48 - Raj Patel: any data egress concerns when Redwood runs replays?
11:54 - Alicia Park: we can run everything inside your VPC with peering and never pull logs out; or if you send anonymized samples we can run on our infra. both options okay.
12:08 - Mike O'Neil: about quantization and model variants: we plan to evaluate a 4-bit quant and an int8 variant if available. will that change latency significantly?
12:18 - Marcus Chen: quant helps memory and throughput but sometimes increases per-token compute. we'll measure unit cost and latency tradeoffs. for heavy long outputs, memory pressure matters more.
12:30 - Samantha Cho: what about streaming responses and user perceived latency?
12:35 - Jonah Ellis: we'll measure time-to-first-byte and chunk latency; streaming usually improves perceived latency even if total generation time is similar.
12:47 - Alicia Park: ok wrapping toward timeline: Alicia to send benchmark template within 48 hours, customer to deliver samples by 2028-01-12, Redwood to run preliminary condensed replay by 2028-01-20, and full benchmark + report by 2028-01-29.
13:05 - Lena Torres: that timeline aligns with our roadmap.
13:10 - Samantha Cho: any costs for the pilot?
13:14 - Alicia Park: we'll propose a pilot SKU — usually a timeboxed Dedicated reservation or hosted credit. i'll include options in the follow-up.
13:22 - Raj Patel: can you include a checklist for firewall/VPC rules we need to open?
13:28 - Jonah Ellis: yes, we'll attach a short network checklist.
13:33 - Mike O'Neil: wrap-up question: how do you validate that the replay is faithful to real user behavior?
13:41 - Marcus Chen: we compare token histograms, session length distributions, and concurrency time-series; we also do correlation tests on response sizes and inter-arrival times. if distributions match within tolerances, the replay is considered faithful.
13:58 - Alicia Park: great. any final questions?
14:02 - Lena Torres: none here, thanks.
14:06 - Samantha Cho: thanks everyone.
14:10 - Alicia Park: thanks all — we'll send artifacts. next meeting tentatively after initial run, we'll schedule a results review.
